title: Paying attention to one thing
keyIdea: Pick one thing and stay with it for a little while. Things will try to pull your eyes away. That is OK. Look back and keep going. A calm spot with just one thing out makes it easier.

kid: Pick one thing, like a book or a puzzle. Look at it. Stay with it a little while.
A bird flies by. A dog barks. Your eyes look away. That is OK! Look back and keep going.
If you stop, you miss the end. Kit the cat looked and looked. Only the last page said where her ball was.
Too many toys make it hard. Put some away. Turn the TV off. Then just one thing is left.
adult: This topic is the start of focused attention: staying with one activity, such as a story, a puzzle or stacking cups, for a few minutes, and coming back to it after a distraction, often with an adult's help. Two- and three-year-olds are easily pulled away; the skill is returning, not never looking up.

The lab gives each part its own action. Children stack cups while a bird tempts them to look, hear a short story to the end despite a beeping TV, return to a fish puzzle after a dog barks, put noisy things away so only the puzzle is left, and keep finding one duck among shiny pictures.

Common mistakes: expecting a toddler to sit still for a long time; adults interrupting a child who is already focused; leaving the TV on in the background, which studies link to shorter, more broken toy play; putting out lots of toys at once, when fewer toys lead to longer play with each; and treating one look away as the end of the activity.

To help, notice what holds your child's interest and join in. When they drift, name the activity and invite them back: "Where were we? The red cup is next." Praise the coming back, not just the finishing.

familyTip: Choose one short picture book and read it in a quiet spot with the TV off. If your child wanders, pause, wait, then say, "Let's see what happens next," and carry on. Do this most days and notice them staying a little longer.

practice.prompt: You are doing a puzzle. A dog barks and you look. What now?
practice.hint: Is the puzzle over just because you looked away?
practice.explain: Looking away is OK. Look back at the puzzle and keep going.

practice.prompt: Your tower has {n} cups. A bird flies by. What helps the tower grow?
practice.hint: The tower only grows when your eyes are on what?
practice.explain: Looking back at the cups lets you add more to your {n} cups. Watching the bird stops the tower.

practice.prompt: Where is it easier to do a puzzle?
practice.hint: Which room has fewer things pulling your eyes away?
practice.explain: Just the puzzle is easiest. Loud TV and lots of toys pull your eyes away.

practice.prompt: A story has {n} pages. You stop on page 2. Do you know the end?
choices: No, the end is on the last page
practice.hint: Where in a book does the story finish?
practice.explain: The end is on the last page of the {n}, so stopping on page 2 means you miss it.

pool.prompt: Story time. A toy beeps. What helps you hear the end?
pool.hint: What will tell you how the story ends?
pool.explain: Looking back at the book lets you hear the end. The toy pulls you away.

pool.prompt: Pip plays with the puzzle, the drum and the ball all at once. Does Pip finish?
choices: No. One thing at a time
pool.hint: Can you finish lots of things if you keep jumping?
pool.explain: Doing it all at once means nothing gets finished. One thing at a time works.

pool.prompt: Too many toys are out. What can help?
pool.hint: Fewer things means fewer pulls on your eyes.
pool.explain: Putting some toys away leaves one thing to focus on.

pool.prompt: You looked away. Is that bad?
pool.hint: What did we do after the dog barked?
pool.explain: Everyone looks away sometimes. The trick is to look back and carry on.

pool.prompt: You put {n} toys away. Now only the puzzle is left. Is it easier?
pool.hint: Count what is left to look at.
pool.explain: With {n} toys put away, only the puzzle is left, so it is easier to stay with it.

pool.prompt: You feel wiggly at story time. What can help?
pool.hint: What helps your body feel calm?
pool.explain: A big breath can help you feel calm so you can keep listening.

pool.prompt: Find the duck! There are {n} shiny things too. What do you do?
pool.hint: What is the one thing you are looking for?
pool.explain: Keep looking for the duck. The {n} shiny things are there to pull your eyes away.

pool.prompt: You got lost in the game. Who can help you come back?
pool.hint: Who is nearby and can help you find your place?
pool.explain: A grown-up can help you find your place and come back to the game.

visual.caption: Does it help you stay with one thing? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: stack cups past a bird, hear a story to the end, come back to a puzzle, clear noisy things and keep your eyes on the duck.
